implementation_notes: The process-wide System.Threading.ThreadPool is the pool, and Task.Run is its idiomatic submission API: it queues a work item on a pooled thread and returns a Task for the result, so no worker loop, queue or thread object is written. The runtime grows the pool itself and SetMinThreads/SetMaxThreads tune it, but the same pool serves timers, async continuations and registered waits, so it is shared infrastructure - keep items short, use async I/O instead of blocking, and move long-blocking work onto dedicated threads. This replaces the classic structure for both fire-and-forget and result-bearing tasks; the classic class only reappears for custom policies (see the Channel<T> variant).
pitfalls: The pool is process-wide: a burst of long-blocking Task.Run items starves timers, continuations and unrelated requests - isolate blocking work on dedicated threads.
Pooled threads keep ThreadStatic/thread-local data between tasks (documented behaviour), so per-task state must be reset or avoided.
ThreadPool threads are background threads: they do not keep the process alive, so a fire-and-forget item can be cut off at exit.

variants.name: Raw ThreadPool.QueueUserWorkItem
variants.implementation_notes: The pre-TPL API: ThreadPool.QueueUserWorkItem(callback, state) posts one item to the shared pool. There is no Task to await, no result and no way to cancel a queued item, so completion has to be signalled by hand with CountdownEvent or ManualResetEventSlim. Use it only in code that cannot take a TPL dependency: Task.Run is the same mechanism with results, composition and cancellation layered on top.
variants.code_sketch:
ThreadPool.QueueUserWorkItem(static state => Process((Job)state!), job);
// completion must be signalled by hand: CountdownEvent / ManualResetEventSlim
pitfalls: A raw pool callback that throws crashes the process: wrap the body in try/catch and report failures explicitly.
SetMaxThreads and SetMinThreads are process-global and can degrade unrelated components that share the pool.

variants.name: Dedicated bounded pool with Channel<T>
variants.implementation_notes: When the shared pool must stay free, or concurrency must be exactly N with a bounded, policy-controlled queue, build a private pool: a bounded Channel<T> as the task queue plus N consumers started with Task.Factory.StartNew(..., TaskCreationOptions.LongRunning) so they get dedicated threads instead of shared pool slots. ChannelOptions control capacity and full-mode (wait/drop/drop-oldest) and Complete() is the shutdown signal; this is the modern replacement for a hand-rolled BlockingCollection pool.
pitfalls: LongRunning tasks are threads you now own: forgetting Complete() and awaiting the workers leaks them past shutdown.
An unbounded channel is the unbounded-queue trap again; size it and pick the full-mode behaviour deliberately so overload has a defined outcome.
